result.markdown: # Tea ![](/images/tea.png){style="width:200px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"} We will have a quick look at the "tea_df". This data shows the annual consumption of tea per capita with a rank based on the highest to lowest consumers. View the __data frame__ and you'll see that the third column has the annual per capita consumption in kilograms (KG) and pounds (LB) with the two values separated by a "_", not ideal. Thankfully we can use the __function__ `gsub()` to fix this. ## gsub() ![](/images/substitute.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"} `gsub()` will look for a specified pattern and replace it with a specified replacement. `gsub()` is only to be used for __strings__. Before fixing our __data frame__ let's see some examples of `gsub()`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #Scalar string with mistake sentence <- "The number 8 is spelt ate" #gsub to print out line with mistake fixed gsub(pattern = "ate", replacement = "eight", sentence) #We can assign the scalar with the fix sentence <- gsub(pattern = "ate", replacement = "eight", sentence) #Vector with unwanted capital As letter_vec <- c("A","Ab","Abc","Abcd") #Replace pattern A with replacement a letter_vec <- gsub(pattern = "A", replacement = "a", letter_vec) #Vector with unwanted info after "_" extra_info_vec <- c("A_some","B_nada","C_stuff","D_nill") #Replace the _ and everything after it with nothing #We signify this with ".*" #This means any character (.) repeated zero or more times (*) gsub(pattern = "_.*", replacement = "", extra_info_vec) #What if we use gsub() with numerics? gsub(pattern = 5, replacement = 2, 1:20) #The output will be strings! ``` ::: ## Regular expressions `.` and `*` are regular expressions. There are many regular expressions but we will only use `.*` to represent "all strings". The best part about this is we can put the `.*` after a specific character to replace the specific character and everything after it. Alternatively we can put the `.*` before a specific character to replace the specific character and everything before it. If you are interested in more regular expressions I would recommend looking at the following resources: - - ## Splitting a column with gsub() ![](/images/weight_measurer.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"} Now we'll split the weight column of "tea_df" into two columns, one for kilograms and one for pounds. ::: {.callout-note} Ensure you have the "tea_df" in your environment before proceeding. See the [tab complete page](/tips_tricks/tab_complete.qmd#file-namespath) if you don't. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #Create a column for lb (pound). We'll copy the KG_LB_annual_per_capita column tea_df$lb <- tea_df$KG_LB_annual_per_capita #For the lb column we'll replace the "_" and everything before it with nothing tea_df$lb <- gsub(pattern = ".*_", replacement = "", tea_df$lb) #Change the column name KG_LB_annual_per_capita to kg colnames(tea_df)[3] <- "kg" #For the kg column we'll replace the "_" and everything after it with nothing tea_df$kg <- gsub(pattern = "_.*", replacement = "", tea_df$kg) #Since the columns initially contained "_" they are string columns #Check if this is correct with the str() function str(tea_df) #Change the kg and lb columns to numerics tea_df$kg <- as.numeric(tea_df$kg) tea_df$lb <- as.numeric(tea_df$lb) #Check with str() to see if it is now numerics str(tea_df) ``` ::: ## gsub() and sub() ![](/images/banana.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"} We've used `gsub()` alt now, but what does gsub actually stand for. The g stands for global and the sub for substitution. This means it will replace all (i.e. global) occurrences of the pattern in the string. See the below example. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fruit <- "Banono" gsub(pattern = "no", replacement = "na", fruit) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Banana" ``` ::: ::: R also has a function called `sub()`. It will only replace the first instance of the pattern in the string. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fruit <- "Banono" sub(pattern = "no", replacement = "na", fruit) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Banano" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: :::
